**Authors:** Sorana Acris, Alejandro J. Ganimian, Elisabeth King, and Kate Marple-Cantrell  
**Venue:** Educational Evaluation and Policy Analysis, 2026. DOI: [10.3102/01623737261468263](https://doi.org/10.3102/01623737261468263)  
**Review Date:** 2026-09-25  
**Model:** GPT-6 via Codex  
**Review Mode:** Retrospective (Reader's Guide)

### Overall Assessment: Useful With Caveats

This school-randomized evaluation provides credible evidence that a supported civic education package in Liberian public primary schools improved curriculum-aligned civic knowledge among pupils observed at follow-up. The reported adjusted effect is 0.379 SD (SE 0.086; p. 11, Table 3). The intervention combined textbooks, teacher training, scheduled instruction, and monitoring, so its success belongs to that package (pp. 6–7). It produced no statistically detectable change in the measured self-reported everyday civic behaviors (p. 15, Table 6). My judgment is that this is useful evidence for the feasibility of civic knowledge instruction in a resource-constrained setting, but readers should qualify claims about general civic competence, universal benefit, pedagogical mechanisms, and democratic consequences. Incomplete follow-up and an unresolved score-normalization ambiguity limit interpretation, while missing replication materials limit independent verification. The strong contribution rating and weak reproducibility rating address different questions: the experiment adds meaningful evidence, but the published documentation does not enable its full reconstruction. Neither the documentation gaps nor the secondary-analysis concerns demonstrate that the main knowledge estimate is wrong.

#### Key Strengths

- The main causal comparison is well founded: schools were randomly assigned within geographic strata, and the principal analysis retains strata controls, baseline adjustment, and school-clustered standard errors (pp. 5–6, 10; p. 11, Table 3). My judgment is that this supports substantial weight on the average knowledge finding, subject to outcome availability.
- The knowledge gain is clearly distinguishable from zero in the reported analysis: 0.379 SD (SE 0.086), with a knowing-domain estimate of 0.370 SD (SE 0.078; p. 11, Table 3). These document learning on the adapted assessment rather than merely improved attitudes toward the program.
- The paper makes an important contextual contribution by testing supported civic instruction in Liberian primary schools and connecting civic-learning research with evidence on instructional materials (pp. 2–3, 6–7, 16–17). Its importance lies in the setting and tested delivery model; an exhaustive claim of priority is unnecessary.
- Classroom observations add evidence about implementation: the adjusted increase in teacher textbook use is 0.402 of class time (SE 0.080; p. 15, Table 5). These observations help characterize the program without identifying which component caused learning.
- The article is navigable, separates knowledge from reported behavior, and reports group means, adjusted contrasts, uncertainty, and follow-up diagnostics (pp. 9–15, Tables 2–6). This makes its central findings more auditable than its broad summary language sometimes suggests.

#### Key Concerns

- Missing outcomes remain a causal limitation: the baseline sample contains 2,107 pupils (p. 6, Table 1), while the assessment analysis contains 1,784 (p. 11, Table 3). The adjusted follow-up difference is −0.006 (SE 0.020), with a joint interaction-test p-value of .323 (p. 9, Table 2). These are reassuring diagnostics, not proof that unobserved outcomes are ignorable; no attrition sensitivity analysis is supplied.
- The reported effect-size denominator is ambiguous: p. 10 says scores are standardized to have “mean zero and SD one at baseline,” whereas the Table 3 note says “mean zero and SD one in the control group” (p. 11). Successive rescaling could reconcile these statements, but is not explained. The supplied article also lacks a documented data-access route, replication code, and sufficient scoring details to reconstruct the knowledge outcome. Online supplements are not bound into the PDF and were unavailable; their contents cannot be assumed deficient.
- Broader outcome and mechanism claims exceed the identified contrast. Engagement covers self-reported helping and law obedience, with responses dichotomized before averaging (p. 15, Table 6); classroom material use is a post-treatment outcome (p. 15, Table 5). My judgment is that neither general behavioral ineffectiveness nor textbook mediation follows from these measures and comparisons.
- Secondary findings deserve less weight than the main mean contrast: upper-tail uncertainty reaches zero in Figure 1 (p. 13), the rural interaction uses county rather than randomization-strata fixed effects (p. 14, Table 4), and the article reports no direct cognitive-domain contrast or multiplicity adjustment (pp. 10–14). These limitations weaken universal-benefit and targeting claims without invalidating the main randomized comparison.
- Policy and literature framing require restraint. Eligibility excludes less accessible schools, and delivery includes external implementation support (pp. 5–8); persistence, routine-delivery costs, and democratic effects are not established (pp. 16–17). The broad claim to first experimental evidence also overlooks earlier community civic education in Liberia; the school-based contribution remains valuable. See the original [Community Empowerment Program report, executive summary](https://poverty-action.org/sites/default/files/publications/blattman_hartman_blair_can_we_teach_peace_ipa_liberia_0.pdf).

#### What to Rely On

- Offering the complete supported program improved the locally adapted civic-knowledge assessment in the reassessed sample: the adjusted overall contrast is 0.379 SD (SE 0.086; p. 11, Table 3), with causal interpretation conditional on the missing-outcome limitation and magnitude subject to the normalization ambiguity.
- The program yielded no statistically detectable short-run change in the particular self-reported behaviors measured: the engagement-index contrast is 0.003 (SE 0.015; p. 15, Table 6). This is a finding about that instrument and follow-up period.
- Observed classrooms used textbooks more and showed greater whole-class engagement under the program (p. 15, Table 5); these are useful implementation findings, not an identified pathway from textbook use to achievement.

#### What to Treat Cautiously

- Claims that civic knowledge cannot change civic behavior or strengthen democracy: the measured everyday behaviors do not establish effects on political participation, democratic tolerance, reconciliation, or later outcomes (p. 15, Table 6; pp. 16–18). The broader literature is not uniformly null either: [USAID’s account of the Georgia evaluation](https://content.govdelivery.com/accounts/USAIDHQ/bulletins/336cde0) reports positive participation and discussion findings; this check concerns the sponsor’s summary, not the full evaluation.
- Claims that higher-order learning was absent or that the cognitive-domain effects differ: reasoning and applying has an estimate of 0.076 SD (SE 0.085), and Table 3 provides no direct between-domain test (p. 11). Statistical inconclusiveness is not a demonstrated zero or a significant difference between effects.
- Claims that all students benefited or that rural targeting is established: Figure 1’s marginal distributions do not identify individual effects and its upper-tail bands include zero (p. 13); the rural interaction of 0.706 (SE 0.238) uses a changed specification (p. 14, Table 4). My methodological judgment is that district-level rural status does not itself require dropping strata controls to estimate the treatment-by-rural interaction.
- Claims that textbooks alone caused the gain, didactic teaching outperforms participatory teaching, or the program will scale cheaply: the trial compares the entire supported package with the control condition, without isolating components or testing alternative pedagogies, long-run sustainability, or cost-effectiveness (pp. 6–7, 16–17; p. 15, Table 5).
- Claims of equivalence to international civic-assessment performance or an unqualified first experiment in post-conflict civic education: the local assessment is adapted rather than demonstrably equated to ICCS (pp. 8–11; p. 11, Table 3), and the earlier [Liberian community experiment](https://poverty-action.org/sites/default/files/publications/blattman_hartman_blair_can_we_teach_peace_ipa_liberia_0.pdf) limits broad novelty claims without negating the school-based contribution.

#### Verification notes

- CONFIRMED — Methods/contribution: the overall effect is 0.379 (SE 0.086), knowing is 0.370 (0.078), and reasoning/applying is 0.076 (0.085), exactly as reported in p. 11, Table 3.
- CONFIRMED — Methods/reproducibility: baseline N = 2,107 (p. 6, Table 1), endline N = 1,784 (p. 11, Table 3), and the adjusted follow-up contrast is −0.006 (0.020), with joint p = .323 (p. 9, Table 2).
- CONFIRMED — Methods/writing/reproducibility: the baseline-versus-control normalization descriptions differ as quoted above; the paper does not explain a rescaling sequence (p. 10; p. 11, Table 3).
- CONFIRMED — Writing: p. 8 describes reassessment as “decreasing by about 1.5 percentage points for each year of age,” but Table 2 reports “Age −0.008 (0.006)” and “Age × Treatment −0.015* (0.008)” (p. 9); my sum is −0.023 for the treatment-group age slope, confirming the review’s correction of the paper’s interpretation.
- CONFIRMED — Methods/writing: visual inspection of p. 13, Figure 1 confirms upper-tail bands include zero; p. 12’s “students at every level of prior achievement benefited” is stronger than its own qualification that gains “become statistically insignificant at the top of the distribution.”
- CONFIRMED — Methods/contribution: teacher textbook use rises by 0.402 (0.080), and the engagement-index contrast is 0.003 (0.015), as verified visually in p. 15, Tables 5 and 6; the latter note confirms dichotomized self-reports.
- CONFIRMED — Methods: the rural interaction is 0.706 (0.238), and its regression substitutes county for strata fixed effects (p. 14, Table 4); the review’s objection to the necessity of that substitution is a methodological judgment.
- CONFIRMED — Literature: the earlier [Community Empowerment Program report](https://poverty-action.org/sites/default/files/publications/blattman_hartman_blair_can_we_teach_peace_ipa_liberia_0.pdf) documents a randomized Liberian community civic-education intervention; [USAID’s Georgia summary](https://content.govdelivery.com/accounts/USAIDHQ/bulletins/336cde0) reports positive school-political participation and discussion outcomes, supporting the review’s limited citation checks.
- COULD NOT CHECK — Writing flags prose-only student textbook-use percentages on p. 12; Table 5’s materials panel is labeled “(teachers)” (p. 15), so no displayed student-use row verifies those percentages; they are not used here.
- COULD NOT CHECK — Reproducibility: full scoring reconstruction, unavailable supplemental instruments, and adherence to the registered plan cannot be verified from the bound article; p. 18 identifies online supplements and on-request results but does not supply them.

### Methods Review
**Rating:** Adequate (high confidence)

School-level randomized assignment, baseline adjustment, and school-clustered inference provide credible evidence that the bundled program improved curriculum-aligned civic knowledge among students reassessed at endline. The main result deserves substantial weight, while incomplete follow-up, limited measurement documentation, and narrower-than-advertised behavioral and distributional evidence constrain broader conclusions about civic competence, mechanisms, and generalizability.

**Strengths:**

- The design matches the central causal question: schools were randomly assigned within geographic strata to receive the program or remain on a wait list, and the primary analysis retains those strata and clusters standard errors at the assignment level (pp. 5–6, 10). School-level assignment also accommodates spillovers among pupils within a treated school as part of the program effect. Baseline comparisons are reassuring, including a joint balance-test p-value of .444 (p. 6, Table 1), although balance tests cannot prove exchangeability.
- The main knowledge result is substantial relative to its reported uncertainty: the adjusted effect is 0.379 SD with a school-clustered standard error of 0.086 (p. 11, Table 3). A normal-approximation confidence interval calculated from those entries is approximately 0.21 to 0.55 SD. The primary result does not depend on the more contestable subgroup or classroom-mechanism analyses.
- Follow-up is transparently examined using treatment status and interactions with baseline characteristics. The control follow-up rate is 0.850 and the adjusted treatment difference is −0.006, with standard error 0.020; the joint interaction test has p = .323 (p. 9, Table 2). These diagnostics reduce concern about obvious differential attrition, even though they cannot establish that missing outcomes are ignorable.
- The assessment draws on an established civic-knowledge framework, is adapted to the taught curriculum, and uses common items to link baseline and endline through an item-response model. Domain analyses use percent-correct scores rather than attempting inadequately supported separate latent-variable models (pp. 8–10). Classroom observations in a randomly selected school subset also provide evidence about implementation beyond participant reports (p. 10; p. 15, Table 5).

**Weaknesses:**

- The reported intent-to-treat estimates use the reassessed panel, rather than outcomes for everyone randomized into the baseline sample: the baseline balance table includes 2,107 pupils, while the outcome table includes 1,784 (p. 6, Table 1; p. 11, Table 3). Comparable aggregate follow-up rates do not rule out treatment-dependent selection on unobserved outcomes. The age-by-treatment follow-up interaction is −0.015 with standard error 0.008 and is marked significant only at the 10% level (p. 9, Table 2). No attrition bounds or missing-outcome sensitivity analysis appear in the supplied paper. My judgment is that this is a residual limitation, not demonstrated evidence that attrition explains the knowledge effect.
- Measurement supports a claim about learning the assessed curriculum more directly than a claim about general civic competence. The main paper does not supply item counts by domain, reliability estimates, item-fit results, or evidence of measurement invariance across treatment groups and waves; detailed assessment materials are assigned to unavailable supplemental appendices (pp. 9–10). There is also an unresolved scale-reference ambiguity: the text says, 'IRT-scaled scores are standardized to have mean zero and SD one at baseline' (p. 10), whereas Table 3 says, 'All scores are standardized to have mean zero and SD one in the control group' and displays endline control values of 0.000 and 1.000 (p. 11, Table 3). These statements could reflect successive rescaling, but the paper does not explain that step. The ambiguity affects interpretation and comparison of the standardized magnitude, rather than by itself refuting a positive treatment contrast.
- Civic engagement is measured with a short set of self-reported everyday behaviors, dichotomized before averaging (p. 10; p. 15, Table 6). High reported engagement, social-desirability error, and discarded response intensity can obscure behavioral change. The index estimate is 0.003 with standard error 0.015, implying an approximate interval of −0.026 to 0.032 in index units; the law-obedience estimate is 0.036 with standard error 0.023, implying approximately −0.009 to 0.081 (my normal-approximation calculations from p. 15, Table 6). The evidence therefore supports no detected change in these reports, not absence of all behavioral effects or proof that knowledge cannot affect subsequent participation.
- The rural analysis unnecessarily drops the randomization-strata fixed effects. The stated reason is that rural status is defined at district level (p. 12; p. 14, Table 4). Methodologically, strata effects absorb the rural main effect, but need not absorb treatment interacted with rural status when treatment varies within strata. The reported rural interaction of 0.706, with standard error 0.238, thus comes from an avoidably different specification (p. 14, Table 4). This does not invalidate random assignment, but makes that policy-relevant subgroup finding less secure than the main result.
- The distributional evidence is more limited than the language of universal benefit suggests. Figure 1 uses smoothed marginal quantiles and baseline-score relationships with bootstrapped confidence intervals, without specifying whether the bootstrap respects school clustering or whether bands are simultaneous (p. 13, Figure 1 and note). Uncertainty reaches the null near the upper tail. Marginal quantile effects cannot establish that every individual benefits, and plotted pointwise results do not establish population-wide stochastic dominance. Likewise, Table 3 does not report a direct test comparing cognitive-domain effects, so differing significance levels alone do not demonstrate that effects differ across domains (p. 11, Table 3).
- Assignment identifies the effect of the complete package, not textbooks alone or the causal contribution of textbook-centered pedagogy (pp. 6–7, 10). Observed material use is a post-treatment outcome, and Table 5 does not identify mediation of achievement. The main text also leaves the subject and comparability of observed control lessons unclear, and does not describe observer blinding or report reliability for the retained observation instrument (p. 10; p. 15, Table 5). These omissions chiefly limit mechanism claims.
- The paper reports numerous domain, subgroup, and instructional-practice tests without describing multiplicity adjustment. It mentions a registered analysis plan and excluded or separately available measures, but the supplied document does not establish registration timing relative to outcome access, specify the full planned outcome hierarchy, or permit assessment of all reporting decisions (p. 18, Notes). Sampling also excludes less accessible schools and depends on pupil presence for baseline assessment (pp. 5, 8). These limits matter more for secondary findings and extrapolation than for the clear primary knowledge contrast.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- Give greatest weight to the average effect of offering the supported instructional package on the locally adapted civic-knowledge assessment for the reassessed sample (p. 11, Table 3). Interpret it subject to the missing-outcome limitation, and retain training, scheduled instruction, and monitoring when describing what was evaluated.
- Read the reasoning-and-applying result as imprecise rather than evidence of no higher-order learning: its estimate of 0.076 and standard error of 0.085 allow an approximate interval from −0.09 to 0.24 SD (my calculation from p. 11, Table 3). Treat the larger factual-knowledge estimate as a suggestive pattern unless a direct cross-domain contrast is available.
- Use Table 6 to characterize short-run changes in the particular self-reported behaviors measured, and use its uncertainty to distinguish undetected effects from tightly excluded effects (p. 15). Do not infer effects on later voting, democratic commitments, or other unmeasured civic behavior.
- Treat rural advantage, universal distributional benefit, and textbook mediation as secondary interpretations requiring additional verification before directing targeting or pedagogical policy (p. 13, Figure 1; p. 14, Table 4; p. 15, Table 5). In particular, verification of the rural interaction with the original strata controls would materially strengthen its interpretation.
- Do not treat the illustrative international assessment comparison as formal score equating: adapting an assessment framework does not demonstrate a common calibrated metric with ICCS (pp. 8–11). Before transporting the effect to other settings, check the score denominator, instrument properties, school-accessibility restrictions, and whether the full implementation support can be reproduced.

**Detailed Commentary:**

This assessment distinguishes document-verifiable evidence from methodological judgment. The paper reports a geographically stratified school experiment, baseline-adjusted outcome regressions, and school-clustered standard errors; these are appropriate foundations for its primary question (pp. 5–6, 10; p. 11, Table 3). The central causal interpretation additionally assumes that outcome availability does not create treatment-dependent selection, that measurement functions comparably across groups, and that cross-school interference does not materially alter the contrast. Limited control exposure is discussed in the text, but self-reported contamination checks do not establish complete isolation (pp. 5–6). The estimated contrast is best understood as an offer effect under the implementation and comparison conditions actually present.

The main knowledge finding is not undermined by a demonstrated assignment or inference failure. Baseline balance and follow-up diagnostics support confidence in it, and the reported uncertainty is sufficiently small to distinguish a positive average assessment effect (p. 6, Table 1; p. 9, Table 2; p. 11, Table 3). Nevertheless, balance on observed characteristics is not proof against missing-outcome bias, and the absence of bound or sensitivity analyses leaves that issue unresolved. It is also important to distinguish learning factual curriculum content from transferring knowledge to unfamiliar problems or later civic life. The paper's internationally framed effect-size analogy does not supply the psychometric evidence needed for cross-assessment equivalence.

The observed increase in teacher textbook use is convincing evidence that classroom materials changed: the adjusted difference is 0.402 of class time with standard error 0.080 (p. 15, Table 5). It is not an estimate of how much achievement would change if textbook use alone changed. Similarly, the randomized program does not compare participatory and didactic approaches, and the broad time-use categories do not exhaust pedagogical quality. Stronger conclusions about which teaching practices are necessary, or about scaling a textbook-only intervention, exceed the identified contrast.

External validity is principally to enrolled, attending pupils in eligible and accessible Liberian public schools operating under the evaluated support arrangements. Average baseline ages are about thirteen in the study sample (p. 6, Table 1), which matters when interpreting the label primary-school intervention across countries. Longer-run persistence, later civic participation, costs, and sustainability under routine implementation are not established by the supplied evaluation. Online supplements and appendices are not bound into the supplied PDF and were unavailable for this review; their instruments, diagnostics, and additional analyses have not been assumed either satisfactory or deficient. On balance, adequate reflects a credible main experiment with meaningful limits on measurement, secondary estimation, and interpretation, rather than a finding that the headline knowledge gain is unreliable.

### Literature Review
**Rating:** Adequate (high confidence)

The paper provides a broad and useful account of civic learning, political socialization, and instructional constraints, and its focus on a primary-school program in Liberia is substantively valuable. Its positioning is less reliable when it generalizes across different civic outcomes or broadens its novelty claim beyond student programs; readers should consult the cited predecessors and omitted Liberian community-education evidence before repeating those claims.

**Strengths:**

- The literature is meaningfully interdisciplinary. Political socialization and comparative civic education inform the motivation and theory of change (pp. 2–3, 7); developmental work on peer influence informs the discussion (p. 16); and economics-of-education research on textbooks and instructional alignment provides a separate implementation perspective (pp. 3, 17). These are substantive connections, not simply a long bibliography.
- The paper acknowledges competing instructional arguments: participatory and experiential approaches versus the knowledge-centered argument associated with Hirsch (p. 2). It also explicitly describes the evidence for participatory approaches as observational or quasi-experimental in the discussion (p. 16), an appropriate distinction from its own randomized evaluation.
- The measurement discussion identifies both an international conceptual source, ICCS, and a local antecedent, Quaynor’s Liberian school research (pp. 8–10). Readers can therefore see how the measured constructs relate to established civic-education research and to the intervention’s curriculum.
- The textbook discussion engages unfavorable earlier findings rather than ignoring them, identifying restricted access and curricular or language mismatch as possible explanations for differences from Kenya and Sierra Leone (pp. 3, 17). The discussion also acknowledges the difficulty of sustaining monitoring at scale (p. 17).

**Weaknesses:**

- The novelty claim loses an essential population restriction. Page 2 claims the first experimental evaluation of effects “on student civic outcomes in a low-income, post-conflict context,” whereas p. 17 states “the first experimental evidence on the effectiveness of civic education in a low-income, post-conflict setting.” The latter wording is too broad: Blattman, Hartman, and Blair’s earlier randomized evaluation of Liberia’s Community Empowerment Program explicitly included civic education, political knowledge, and participation. This is a community-program antecedent, not a refutation of the narrower school-based claim. Its omission matters because it supplies directly relevant local evidence. Verified against the original report, executive summary and section 6.3: [Can We Teach Peace and Conflict Resolution?](https://poverty-action.org/sites/default/files/publications/blattman_hartman_blair_can_we_teach_peace_ipa_liberia_0.pdf).
- Some citations grouped as evidence about behavior concern different outcomes. Pages 3, 7, and 16 invoke Finkel and Ernst (2005) when interpreting weak behavioral effects, but that study’s reported outcomes include political knowledge, democratic values, skills, and approval of participation. Approval is not enacted participation. Its findings do support the distinction between learning content and changing broader orientations, but provide less direct support for the specific behavioral generalization than the citation grouping suggests. This distinction is verified in the original article’s abstract and conclusion: [Finkel and Ernst](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1467-9221.2005.00421.x).
- The treatment of NORC (2019) is incomplete. The report is cited as consistent with difficulty changing civic behavior (p. 3) and with weaker or null behavioral effects (p. 7), without describing its positive engagement findings. USAID’s own account of that evaluation reports improvements in participation in school politics and political discussion. This does not imply success on every outcome, but it means the study is mixed evidence rather than a simple supporting null. I verified the sponsor’s account, not the inaccessible full evaluation: [USAID’s civic-education evidence digest](https://content.govdelivery.com/accounts/USAIDHQ/bulletins/336cde0).
- The literature on competing conceptions of citizenship is underdeveloped. Helping others and obeying laws are the engagement outcomes (p. 15, Table 6), but they do not exhaust democratic participation, political voice, or challenges to exclusion. Westheimer and Kahne’s omitted distinction among personally responsible, participatory, and justice-oriented citizenship directly changes how these outcomes should be interpreted. This is an interpretive limitation, not evidence that the selected measures are intrinsically invalid. Their mixed-method study also supplies a qualitative perspective on what different civic curricula aim to produce: [What Kind of Citizen?](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/243786974_What_Kind_of_Citizen_The_Politics_of_Educating_for_Democracy).
- The paper does not give its closest intellectual antecedents enough analytical attention. Green et al. (2011) is cited mainly as an example of prior experimental or participatory civic instruction (pp. 2–3, 16), although its central finding was that increased constitutional knowledge did not produce increased support for civil liberties. That makes it particularly relevant to the limits of a knowledge-to-democratic-outcomes theory. Likewise, Finkel and Ernst already distinguished knowledge gains from changes in broader democratic orientations. The new contribution is stronger causal evidence in a different school and resource setting, rather than discovery of that distinction. Green et al.’s result is verified in the original abstract: [Green et al.](https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/abs/10.1017/S0022381611000107).

**Guidance for Readers:**

- Cite this article for the effects of a supported, textbook-centered civic-education program in Liberian public primary schools. Preserve the student and school setting when describing its novelty; the earlier Community Empowerment Program is essential companion evidence for any broader claim about experimental civic education in post-conflict Liberia.
- Read Green et al. (2011) and Finkel and Ernst (2005) alongside this paper, keeping knowledge, attitudes, skills, intentions, and behavior separate. Check NORC (2019) directly before repeating a general claim that its engagement findings were null; the available sponsor summary indicates a more mixed picture.
- Use Westheimer and Kahne (2004) to interpret the helping and law-obedience outcomes as a particular conception of citizenship. Read Quaynor (2012), already cited for measurement, for local context rather than assuming international constructs and Liberian civic practices are interchangeable.
- Treat the textbook comparison as evidence about a delivery package and its context. The program also included training, scheduled instruction, and monitoring (pp. 6–7), so its contrast with earlier textbook studies does not by itself establish that textbook relevance or access explains the different results.

**Detailed Commentary:**

My rating is adequate because the article engages central research traditions, recognizes a real contextual gap, and discusses evidence that does not uniformly favor its intervention. The weaknesses concern the precision and depth of the synthesis more than a wholesale absence of relevant scholarship. Statements above about which studies are cited and which outcomes are measured are verifiable from the article; judgments about the importance of omissions and the appropriate scope of its contribution are my assessment.

The omitted Liberian community-education experiment is especially consequential. It studied a different population and intervention, so it should not erase the school-based contribution. Nevertheless, it examined civic knowledge, rights, participation, and conflict in the same post-conflict national setting. The article cites Blair, Blattman, and Hartman’s separate Patterns of Conflict and Cooperation report as contextual evidence (p. 4; reference on p. 18), but does not engage the Community Empowerment Program evaluation. The earlier trial’s mixed findings also caution against organizing the field around a simple opposition between textbook knowledge and participatory behavior.

The primary-school contribution should also be separated from a claim about very young children. The students’ mean age was approximately 13 in both groups (p. 6, Table 1). Thus, adolescent political socialization is directly relevant despite their primary-school enrollment. The paper deserves credit for recognizing this developmental context on p. 16. In my judgment, the peer-influence literature offers a plausible interpretation of the findings, but does not establish that peer norms explain this program’s behavioral results.

The literature supports asking whether civic knowledge has longer-term consequences, but the article’s appeal to predictive associations on p. 3 should not be read as evidence that intervention-induced learning will cause future democratic participation. Its own call for longitudinal assessment on p. 16 appropriately leaves that question open. Similarly, alignment with ICCS gives the study a recognizable conceptual framework; it does not alone establish equivalence between a locally adapted assessment and the international assessment scale.

I read the complete supplied article, including its references. External checks were targeted rather than an exhaustive search of all civic-education experiments. I verified selected original publications or their abstracts and the original Liberian community-program report; the NORC concern is explicitly limited to the sponsor’s summary. I have not independently established the exhaustive claim that Mahéo is the only earlier primary-level RCT. Online supplements and appendices are not bound into the supplied article and were unavailable for this review, so their additional measurement and qualitative material cannot resolve the positioning issues here.

### Writing Review
**Rating:** Adequate (high confidence)

The article is clearly organized, and its central account of improved civic knowledge with no statistically detectable change in measured civic behaviors is readily recoverable from the main tables. However, several consequential exposition problems require readers to check the exhibits: an interaction is misinterpreted, descriptions of scaling and covariate adjustment are not reconciled, and some summary language overstates the breadth or certainty of the evidence.

**Strengths:**

- Organization is effective: Experiment, Data, Empirical Strategy, and outcome-specific Results sections provide a clear route from the intervention to the evidence (pp. 4–12). The descriptions of content versus cognitive domains (pp. 8–10) help distinguish knowledge about civic participation from actual civic behavior.
- The headline knowledge estimates are faithfully reported. The abstract (p. 1) and Results (p. 11) round the adjusted overall effect of 0.379 SD and the knowing-domain effect of 0.370 SD appropriately; both values are directly verifiable in Table 3 (p. 11, panels A and C). The content-domain discussion also distinguishes supported gains from statistically inconclusive results.
- The main tables generally provide useful interpretive information: Table 3 distinguishes IRT-based overall scores from percent-correct subscales and specifies adjustment; Table 4 identifies the changed fixed effects for the rural comparison; and Table 6 explains response dichotomization and construction of the engagement index (pp. 11, 14–15). Group means and regression-adjusted differences are separate, so their failure to equal simple subtraction is explained rather than a numerical error.
- Figure 1 separates endline-quantile comparisons from effects conditional on baseline achievement and displays uncertainty bands and a visible zero line (p. 13). The rural heterogeneity discussion explicitly advises caution about its different specification (p. 12; Table 4, p. 14), while the discussion acknowledges possible engagement ceiling effects and challenges in sustaining monitoring at scale (pp. 16–17).

**Weaknesses:**

- The abstract overcompresses the engagement result and its scope. It says the program had "no impact on students’ civic engagement" (p. 1), whereas the Results say "no significant impact on students’ self-reported civic engagement behaviors" (p. 12). Table 6 (p. 15) concerns helping schoolmates, helping neighbors, and obeying community laws, with estimated differences of −0.034 (SE 0.021), 0.006 (0.019), and 0.036 (0.023), respectively. These are verifiable estimates with uncertainty, not demonstrated absence of all civic-engagement effects. In my judgment, the abstract needs to be read through the narrower measurement description and the qualified Results wording.
- The reported score units are not fully reconciled. The Data section says "IRT-scaled scores are standardized to have mean zero and SD one at baseline" (p. 10); the Table 3 note says "All scores are standardized to have mean zero and SD one in the control group" (p. 11), whose endline overall-score entry is "0.000 [1.000]." A further standardization could reconcile these statements, but it is not explained. This is a documented ambiguity about the denominator of the reported effect, not proof that the estimate was computed incorrectly.
- The general specification description conflicts with the table-specific accounts of adjustment. Page 10 says, "All analyses control for students’ baseline assessment scores in all program effect calculations." Table 5 instead describes "controls for randomization strata," and Table 6 specifies "controls for randomization strata and baseline measures of civic engagement" (both p. 15). Readers cannot tell from these descriptions whether baseline assessment scores were additionally included or whether the universal sentence overstates the actual specifications.
- The attrition paragraph mistakes a between-group difference in age slopes for the age slope within the treatment group. Page 8 describes treatment students’ likelihood of reassessment as "decreasing by about 1.5 percentage points for each year of age." Table 2, panel B (p. 9), instead reports "Age −0.008 (0.006)" and "Age × Treatment −0.015* (0.008)." Adding those coefficients gives a treatment-group slope of −0.023, or about −2.3 percentage points per year; this is my calculation from the table. The interaction is the additional decline relative to controls. Moreover, the prose calls the difference "statistically significant" without specifying that its single star denotes significance only at the table’s 10% threshold (Table 2, p. 9).
- The instructional-practices narrative includes student material-use figures that the cited exhibit does not display. Page 12 states that students used textbooks for "63% of class time" in treatment schools and "2% of class time" in control schools, within its discussion of Table 5. Yet Table 5, panel B, is explicitly headed "Allocation of time using different materials (teachers)" (p. 15); its other panels concern time on task and student engagement, not students’ textbook use. There is no matching student-use row in the supplied PDF, so those prose-only percentages and their reported significance cannot be checked against an exhibit. This is missing displayed support, not evidence that the percentages are false.
- Distributional findings are narrated more conclusively than their uncertainty warrants. Page 12 says the baseline-score analysis "confirm[s] that students at every level of prior achievement benefited," but the same paragraph acknowledges gains "which become statistically insignificant at the top of the distribution." Figure 1 (p. 13, panels A and B) visibly includes zero within the confidence bands near the upper tail. Positive fitted differences support the abstract’s account of a broadly positive pattern, but the stronger universal-benefit wording and the unqualified first-order-dominance claim (pp. 11–12) should not be read as an established effect at every percentile or for every student.
- The prose sometimes turns descriptive patterns into stronger explanations or policy conclusions. The introduction says observations suggest knowledge gains "were driven by textbook-centered instruction rather than shifts in pedagogy" (pp. 2–3), while Table 5 (p. 15) shows material use, time allocation, and engagement rather than an identified mediation pathway. Likewise, "making knowledge-building programs more scalable and sustainable" (p. 16) and "a scalable model for strengthening democratic foundations" (p. 17) go beyond what the knowledge and engagement exhibits establish (Tables 3 and 6, pp. 11 and 15). These are interpretive extensions, in my judgment; the later monitoring-cost qualification on p. 17 is more measured.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- For an efficient reading, start with the intervention description (pp. 6–7), the outcome definitions (pp. 8–10), and Tables 3 and 6 (pp. 11 and 15). These establish what was offered, what was measured, and the central findings. The broad democratic-background discussion (pp. 1–5) and repeated comparisons with textbook interventions in the Discussion (pp. 16–17) can be skimmed once that context is understood.
- Before quoting standardized effects or the adjustment strategy, read the relevant table note alongside p. 10 and preserve the unresolved scaling/specification qualifications. Before quoting the age-related attrition result, use Table 2 (p. 9) and distinguish the age-by-treatment interaction from the treatment-group age slope.
- Read Figure 1 (p. 13) with its confidence bands, and keep its endline-quantile and baseline-achievement panels conceptually separate. For classroom findings, use the displayed teacher-material and engagement rows in Table 5 (p. 15); treat the student textbook-use percentages on p. 12 as unverified against the supplied exhibits.
- Do not substitute the abstract for the engagement measurement section and Table 6 (pp. 10 and 15). Also retain the qualifications on rural heterogeneity, ceiling effects, and monitoring costs (pp. 12, 16–17). The online appendices are not bound into this PDF and were unavailable for this review, so their instrument examples and additional implementation documentation cannot resolve the gaps here.

**Detailed Commentary:**

Assessment basis: I read the complete article, including notes and references, and visually checked the principal exhibits and the passages bearing on the discrepancies above. The rating is adequate because the paper is navigable and the central reported estimates match the main outcome table; the lapses nonetheless affect how precisely readers can state the results. Documented wording and table entries are identified above; conclusions about overstatement and the resulting reading burden are my judgments.

A further interpretive caution concerns the effect-size translations on p. 11. The text describes the overall effect as moving the median student "approximately 15 percentile points higher" and as "roughly equivalent to a 38-point increase on the ICCS scale." The source study estimate is 0.379 SD in Table 3, panel A (p. 11); neither that table nor Figure 1 (p. 13) directly reports those translated quantities. The percentile statement is consistent with a normal-distribution benchmark rather than a directly reported individual rank movement, and the ICCS comparison is an analogy rather than demonstrated test equating. The paper explains that its instrument was adapted from ICCS and aligned to the Liberian curriculum (pp. 8–10), but it does not establish a common calibrated metric with the international assessment. In my judgment, the analogies are helpful for orientation only if readers retain these distinctions.

The bound article also leaves some measurement information outside the main narrative. The engagement response coding and index definition are recoverable in Table 6’s note (p. 15), but representative knowledge items and fuller instrument-adaptation details are deferred to unavailable online appendices (pp. 9–10). Page 18 further notes that attitude results and findings from an excluded classroom-observation instrument are available upon request. These disclosures help identify the limits of the displayed record; their contents were not assumed in this writing review.

### Contribution Review
**Rating:** Strong (high confidence)

This paper makes a strong, bounded contribution by providing randomized evidence that a supported, textbook-centered civic education program can improve curriculum-aligned civic knowledge in Liberia's resource-constrained public primary schools. Its principal novelty is the population, setting, and implementation evidence rather than a new method or a new knowledge-to-behavior theory; the evidence supports factual learning more clearly than broader civic competence, behavioral change, or democratic consolidation.

**Strengths:**

- The study addresses an important gap at the intersection of primary education, civic learning, and a low-income post-conflict setting. Relative to the literature described in the paper, experimental evidence for this combination is unusually scarce (pp. 2–3). School-level random assignment provides a substantially firmer basis for judging the implemented program than the observational associations discussed in that literature (pp. 5–6, 10). This assessment of its standing is based on the paper's account of prior work, not an independently verified claim of priority.
- The central result is substantively useful: the reported overall assessment effect is 0.379 SD (SE 0.086), with a knowing-domain effect of 0.370 SD (SE 0.078; p. 11, Table 3). These findings demonstrate that meaningful gains on the local civic assessment are possible under a program built around textbooks, teacher preparation, scheduled instruction, and monitoring. The contribution is a credible example of successful delivery and learning under resource constraints, rather than simply an argument that civic education deserves attention.
- The outcome distinctions help readers avoid treating all civic outcomes as interchangeable. The reasoning-and-applying estimate is smaller and statistically inconclusive (p. 11, Table 3), while the engagement index shows little estimated change (p. 15, Table 6). Knowledge about participation and reported participation-related behavior are kept empirically separate, making the paper useful for evaluating what a civic curriculum actually achieves.
- Classroom observations add valuable evidence about instruction in an understudied subject. The program increased teacher textbook use and whole-class engagement without a detectable change in the broad allocation of instructional time (p. 15, Table 5). Together with the implementation description (pp. 6–8), this documents how the tested model operated and makes the result more informative for practice than a test-score effect alone.

**Weaknesses:**

- The randomized contrast identifies the effect of the entire supported program, not textbook provision alone, curricular alignment alone, or didactic teaching relative to participatory instruction (pp. 5–7, 10). The classroom observations do not identify which component caused the learning gains. Accordingly, the comparison with less successful textbook interventions in other settings is suggestive about implementation, not a causal explanation of why those studies and this one differ (pp. 3, 16–17).
- The civic-engagement contribution is narrower than the broad label suggests. The reported outcomes concern self-reported help with schoolwork, help for neighbors, and obedience to community laws, dichotomized by reported frequency (p. 15, Table 6); these do not directly measure political participation, democratic tolerance, or intergroup reconciliation. The paper acknowledges limited headroom in reported behaviors (pp. 15–16), and attitude results are not presented in the article (p. 18, note 3). Thus, the null findings constrain claims about these measured behaviors but do not establish that civic education cannot affect civic engagement generally.
- Transportability is limited by the sampling and delivery conditions. The sample excludes logistically inaccessible schools and applies classroom-size eligibility restrictions; the intervention also benefits from NGO implementation and recurring monitoring (pp. 5–8). Primary-school status should not be equated with a sample of young children: mean age is approximately 13 (p. 6, Table 1). These features matter when transferring the findings to remote schools, younger cohorts, or ordinary ministry delivery.
- Policy significance beyond immediate learning remains prospective. The paper does not establish durable learning, subsequent political behavior, cost-effectiveness, or sustained implementation after external support ends (pp. 8, 16–17). Its explicit cautions about national context and monitoring costs are appropriate, but the claims about scalability and strengthening democratic foundations extend beyond outcomes directly evaluated.
- The knowledge assessment is aligned with the intervention's curriculum, and the article does not establish that its scores are equated to the international ICCS scale (pp. 8–11). The international-score analogy should therefore not carry the significance argument. Online appendices and supplements are unavailable for this review; the item examples and instrument-development details referenced on pp. 9–10 cannot be inspected, limiting assessment of how broadly the measured learning extends beyond taught content.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- Cite this paper as randomized evidence that the implemented Liberian civic education package improved curriculum-aligned civic knowledge, particularly factual knowledge, in the assessed public-primary-school population (p. 11, Table 3). Retain the training, instruction, and monitoring components when describing the treatment.
- Cite the engagement result as no statistically detectable short-run change in the specified self-reported everyday behaviors. The engagement-index estimate is 0.003 (SE 0.015; p. 15, Table 6). Do not turn this into proof of no behavioral effect at any horizon or into a conclusion about voting, democratic attitudes, or social cohesion, which the reported measures do not establish.
- Use the classroom findings to describe the program's observed instructional pattern (p. 15, Table 5), not to claim that textbook use mediated the achievement effect or that participatory pedagogy is ineffective. The trial contains no experimental comparison that resolves those questions.
- Treat the paper as an important reference for the feasibility of supported civic knowledge instruction in comparable settings, rather than as evidence that national expansion will be inexpensive or equally effective. Durability, routine-delivery costs, effects in excluded schools, and the added value of participatory complements remain open questions (pp. 5–8, 16–17).
- Describe the study as filling a rare experimental evidence gap on the basis of the literature presented in the article (pp. 2–3). An unqualified claim that it is the first or the best available study across all civic education settings would require a broader literature verification than this document-only assessment permits.

**Detailed Commentary:**

My judgment is that the contribution merits strong because the question has practical stakes and the trial supplies credible evidence in a population and institutional setting poorly represented in the literature it reviews. The novelty is primarily evidentiary: a familiar distinction between acquiring knowledge and changing behavior is tested in Liberian primary education, alongside unusually useful implementation and classroom information. The paper is not a methodological innovation, and its behavioral pattern largely reinforces prior findings as described by the authors. Neither limitation makes its contribution weak.

The most defensible update for readers is that a supported civic curriculum can produce factual learning without an intervention centered on major pedagogical reform. The experiment does not settle whether a different pedagogy would produce larger gains, whether textbooks without implementation support would work, or whether factual learning is sufficient for later democratic participation. The distributional evidence also suggests that learning gains are not confined to the highest achievers (p. 13, Figure 1), but it should not be read as proof that every student benefits.

Relative to the prior work described in the article, this is an especially relevant causal reference for the narrow question of this program's effects on local civic knowledge. The supplied document does not support ranking it as the best evidence for civic education in general. Its strongest follow-on value is to establish a tested instructional model against which persistence, behavioral transfer, alternative pedagogies, and delivery under ordinary public-system conditions can be assessed. The authors draw several useful boundaries, including caution about generalization and the sustainability of monitoring (p. 17); readers should retain those qualifications when citing the broader policy implications. These judgments separate findings directly documented in the trial's tables from my assessment of their importance and reach.

### Reproducibility Review
**Rating:** Weak (high confidence)

The paper makes the randomized design, main treatment-effect specification, sample retention, and tabulated estimates reasonably transparent, but the supplied article does not provide a documented data-access route, replication code, or enough measurement detail to reconstruct the central knowledge outcomes. Missing score-construction instructions and an unresolved normalization ambiguity materially limit independent reproduction; this assessment applies to the supplied paper, not to the unavailable online supplements.

**Strengths:**

- The sampling and assignment descriptions identify the geographic frame, school eligibility and exclusions, within-school classroom and student sampling, county/district stratification, and the fallback procedure when a grade had too few students (pp. 5–8, Sample, Randomization, and Data Collection and Attrition). Sample retention is auditable at the aggregate level: the baseline table reports 2,107 students (p. 6, Table 1), while the endline assessment table reports 1,784, split into 936 control and 848 treatment students (p. 11, Table 3). Follow-up regressions disclose baseline predictors, treatment interactions, clustered standard errors, and a joint test (p. 9, Table 2).
- The principal estimand and regression are explicit: the effect of assignment to the program, estimated by ordinary least squares with randomization-stratum fixed effects, baseline adjustment, and school-clustered standard errors (p. 10, Equation 1). The assessment table specifies overall baseline IRT adjustment versus domain-specific baseline percent-correct adjustment (p. 11, Table 3 note). The heterogeneity table identifies its interaction models and the substitution of county fixed effects for strata in the rural specification (p. 14, Table 4 note).
- Results tables distinguish descriptive means and standard deviations from adjusted effects and standard errors. For example, the main knowledge effect is 0.379 with standard error 0.086 (p. 11, Table 3, overall assessment row). The engagement table states the response dichotomization and construction of the mean index, making these outcomes substantially easier to reconstruct than the knowledge scores (p. 15, Table 6 note).
- The paper identifies the assessment and observation frameworks, describes pooling assessment waves and linking through shared items, and distinguishes IRT scoring from domain percent-correct scoring (pp. 8–10). It also gives an identifiable AEA registry record for the stated pre-analysis plan and discloses that attitude results and excluded observation-tool results are available upon request (p. 18, Notes). These are useful verification leads, although the underlying materials were not available for this review.

**Weaknesses:**

- The data are original study assessments, surveys, observations, and implementation records rather than an identified downloadable dataset (pp. 8–10). The supplied article contains no data-availability statement, repository address, documented restricted-access application, or data-use-agreement procedure; nor does it explain whether sharing is prohibited. The corresponding-author contact provides a way to inquire, but not an established access pathway. The absence of public child-level data is not itself the problem: the missing pathway and documentation prevent a reader from knowing how verification could proceed.
- No analysis-code deposit, code-on-request statement, software/package versions, or executable workflow is identified in the supplied paper. In particular, the IRT description does not identify the estimation implementation, person-score estimator, identification constraints, item parameters, treatment of omitted responses, or fit/convergence checks (pp. 9–10, Student Civic Knowledge). The complete instruments, answer keys, item-to-domain map, and shared-item map are not supplied; the text instead points to online appendices for framework and item information. A researcher with raw responses would still have to make consequential choices to regenerate the headline outcome.
- Score normalization is not unambiguously documented. The methods say, 'IRT-scaled scores are standardized to have mean zero and SD one at baseline' (p. 10, Student Civic Knowledge), whereas the results note says, 'All scores are standardized to have mean zero and SD one in the control group' (p. 11, Table 3 note). The endline control mean and standard deviation are 0.000 and 1.000 (p. 11, Table 3, overall assessment row). These statements could reflect successive rescaling, but the article does not describe that sequence or identify the reference wave and sample for every transformation. Consequently, the denominator of the reported standardized effect cannot be reconstructed confidently from the prose alone.
- The paper explains overall recruitment and retention but does not provide a record-level sample-construction recipe: wave-linkage rules, handling of incomplete instruments or missing covariates, and the membership/coding of randomization strata are not supplied (pp. 5–10). The household-assets index used in follow-up and heterogeneity analyses is not given a construction formula, and the rule for classifying districts as rural is not operationalized (p. 9, Table 2; p. 14, Table 4). The classroom-observation description does not specify which lessons were selected in control schools or how observations across classrooms were aggregated into the analyzed outcomes (p. 10, Instructional Practices; p. 15, Table 5). These are specific reconstruction gaps rather than a failure to describe the overall design.
- Baseline adjustment outside the assessment analysis requires clarification. The empirical-strategy text states, 'All analyses control for students’ baseline assessment scores in all program effect calculations' (p. 10), but the engagement note describes 'controls for randomization strata and baseline measures of civic engagement' (p. 15, Table 6 note), and the instructional-practices note describes 'controls for randomization strata' (p. 15, Table 5 note). The table notes may be intended to define outcome-specific exceptions; they do not establish whether baseline knowledge scores were additionally included or, for observations, how they would be aggregated.
- The distributional figure names local polynomial regression and bootstrapped confidence intervals but omits bandwidths, polynomial degree, kernel, percentile/tie handling, bootstrap resampling unit, replication count, and seed (p. 13, Figure 1 note). Its curves and uncertainty bands therefore cannot be regenerated exactly from the description. The article also leaves attitude results and the evidence behind exclusion of the alternative observation instrument to requests or online material (p. 18, Notes), limiting verification of the full outcome-selection record.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- Before attempting replication, request the data-access conditions and an analysis package containing deidentified data or an approved restricted-access route, a codebook, linkage and sample flags, strata identifiers, and scripts with software versions. If participant confidentiality precludes transfer, ask whether the authors or a trusted custodian can execute independently supplied code or provide a synthetic-data workflow.
- Prioritize regeneration of the main assessment table: obtain the instruments, scoring keys, item/domain and cross-wave mappings, missing-response rules, fitted IRT specification and scoring method, and exact normalization constants. Check explicitly whether the table uses baseline-control, endline-control, or another reference standard deviation before relying on its standardized magnitude (pp. 10–11, Table 3).
- Reconcile the regression scripts with the outcome-specific table notes, rebuild the baseline and follow-up samples, and reproduce the balance and attrition diagnostics before comparing treatment effects (p. 6, Table 1; p. 9, Table 2; p. 11, Table 3; p. 15, Tables 5–6). For engagement, verify response recoding, baseline adjustment, and index handling when an item is missing; for observations, obtain the lesson-selection and aggregation rules.
- Consult the registry record and dated plan identified in the paper, together with the unavailable online appendices, to check planned outcomes, exclusions, and analytic changes; the printed registration claim alone does not verify adherence. Request the distributional-analysis code and school-level bootstrap details before leaning on the claims about effects throughout the achievement distribution (p. 13, Figure 1). The excluded outcomes and exact score construction remain effectively unverifiable from the supplied article alone.

**Detailed Commentary:**

Document-verifiable findings are that the article provides an explicit main regression, interpretable outcome tables with uncertainty and sample sizes, aggregate sample-flow information, and named measurement frameworks, while providing no documented data-access procedure or code/software environment in the supplied PDF. I read the entire paper and inspected the model, assessment table, distributional figure, and observation/engagement tables directly in the PDF. Online supplemental material is announced on p. 18 but is not bound into the supplied article and was unavailable for this review; I therefore do not infer that it lacks instruments, code, or additional diagnostics. The registry and on-request results were likewise not independently inspected. My judgment is that 'weak' is warranted because reproducing the central knowledge finding requires unavailable item-level construction details and clarification of its scale, even if a replicator could obtain the raw data. This is more consequential than the ordinary limitation that confidential data cannot be publicly posted. 'Insufficient' would be too severe: readers can understand the experiment, identify the principal estimand, inspect the reported precision, and reconstruct substantial portions of the regression logic. The rating concerns independent verifiability, not evidence that the reported estimates are incorrect. Confidence is high about the documentation supplied, with uncertainty about whether the inaccessible materials would resolve these gaps.
